content.intro: Learn right join and full outer join through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of right join and full outer join is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

items.title: Right joins
items.text: Right joins determines how rows from related sources are matched. Write the join predicate explicitly and check whether multiple matches can multiply rows; use a LEFT JOIN when unmatched left-side records must remain visible.

items.title: Full outer joins
items.text: Full outer joins determines how rows from related sources are matched. Write the join predicate explicitly and check whether multiple matches can multiply rows; use a LEFT JOIN when unmatched left-side records must remain visible.

items.title: Retaining unmatched rows from both sides
items.text: Retaining unmatched rows from both sides determines how rows from related sources are matched. Write the join predicate explicitly and check whether multiple matches can multiply rows; use a LEFT JOIN when unmatched left-side records must remain visible.

items.title: Identifying missing relationships
items.text: Identifying missing relationships requires deliberate handling of absent or unknown values. In SQL, NULL is not the same as zero or an empty string; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for direct tests and check how expressions and aggregates propagate unknowns.

items.title: Availability and syntax differences
items.text: Availability and syntax differences helps you combine related tables correctly, predict matched and unmatched rows, and diagnose incorrect row multiplication or missing relationships. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT o.order_id, c.full_name, o.order_date, o.total_amount
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.order_date DESC, o.order_id DESC;
content_blocks.expected_output: Each order is paired with its customer through the foreign-key relationship. The unique tie-breaker makes the requested order deterministic.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
